decks.title: Special Purpose Books — Part 1: Petty Cash Book, Purchases Book and Sales Book
goals: Prepare an analytical petty cash book on the imprest system, balance it, find the reimbursement and post the column totals
Record credit purchases and credit sales of goods in simple and columnar day books, deducting trade discount
Separate transactions that belong in the purchases and sales books from those that go to the cash book or the journal proper, and post the books to the ledger

slides.heading: Special books: petty cash, purchases and sales
slides.body_md: Part 1: the **petty cash book** on the imprest system, and the **purchases book** and **sales book** in simple and columnar form.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: petty expenses go to the petty cash book, credit purchases to the purchases book and credit sales to the sales book, and the totals are posted to the ledger
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Welcome. Every business has small daily payments and a great many credit purchases and credit sales. Writing each one in the journal would be slow and repetitive, so accountants keep special books. In this part we meet the petty cash book, the purchases book and the sales book, using imagined firms.

slides.heading: Why a business keeps special books
bullets: A **special book** records only one kind of transaction.
It is totalled, and the **totals** are posted to the ledger, so posting is far lighter.
Several clerks can write different books at the same time.

rows: Small cash payments of the office
Credit purchases of goods for resale
Every entry that fits no other book
Each entry posted on its own

visual.alt: Table of the special books: petty cash book, purchases book, sales book, the two returns books and the journal proper, each with what it records, its source document and where its total is posted
visual.caption: Special books at a glance

slides.narration: A special book is a subsidiary book that records one kind of transaction. The petty cash book takes small payments. The purchases book takes credit purchases of goods, and the sales book credit sales. Two more books take returns, and the journal proper takes whatever fits nowhere else. Each book is totalled, and the totals are posted to the ledger.

slides.heading: Petty cash and the imprest system
bullets: **Petty cash** is the small cash kept for postage, fares, tea and similar payments.
Under the **imprest system** the petty cashier gets a **fixed sum**, the imprest.
At the end of the period he is given **exactly what he spent**, which restores the sum.

nodes.label: The book is totalled and balanced
Head cashier reimburses what was spent
The float is the imprest again

visual.alt: Cycle of the imprest system: the head cashier gives the fixed imprest, the petty cashier pays against vouchers, the book is totalled and balanced, the amount spent is reimbursed and the float is back to the imprest
visual.caption: One cycle of the imprest system

slides.narration: Petty cash is the small cash kept for postage, fares, tea and other minor payments. Under the imprest system the head cashier gives the petty cashier a fixed sum. He pays out against vouchers. At the end of the period the head cashier repays exactly what was spent, so the petty cashier starts again with the same fixed sum.

slides.heading: The analytical petty cash book
slides.body_md: Each payment is written in the **Total** column and again in the **analysis column** of its head. A voucher for two heads is split between two columns. The **receipts** column holds the balance in hand and the cash received.

rows: By Auto fare to the bank

visual.alt: First lines of an analytical petty cash book of Tanjore Brass Emporium, an imagined firm: the receipts column, date, particulars, voucher number, a total column and an analysis column each for postage, stationery, conveyance, refreshments and sundries
visual.caption: Format of the analytical petty cash book (first lines only)

slides.narration: The analytical petty cash book has a receipts column on the left and a total column for payments. Beside the total are analysis columns, one for each head of expense, such as postage, stationery and conveyance. Every payment appears in the total column and again in its own head. A voucher that covers two heads is split between two columns.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a week of petty cash
slides.body_md: **Tanjore Brass Emporium**, an imagined firm, keeps an imprest of ₹2,000. On 3 January 2028, ₹150 is in hand, so the head cashier gives ₹1,850. Eight vouchers are paid in the week. Prepare the book.
bullets: Total payments ₹1,465; balance carried down ₹535.
Reimbursement on 9 January: ₹1,465.

rows: By Auto fare to the bank
By Fare and porter at the railway station

visual.alt: Analytical petty cash book of Tanjore Brass Emporium for the week of 3 to 8 January 2028: eight vouchers analysed under five heads, total payments of one thousand four hundred sixty five rupees, a balance carried down of five hundred thirty five rupees and a reimbursement of one thousand four hundred sixty five rupees
visual.caption: Tanjore Brass Emporium: imprest ₹2,000

slides.narration: The week begins with rupees one hundred fifty in hand and rupees one thousand eight hundred fifty received, which makes the imprest of rupees two thousand. Eight vouchers are written in the total column and in their heads. Payments come to rupees one thousand four hundred sixty five, so rupees five hundred thirty five is carried down. The head cashier then repays rupees one thousand four hundred sixty five.

slides.heading: Quick check: balance in hand
slides.body_md: Subtract what was spent from the imprest.
slides.narration: Start from the fixed imprest and take away the amount spent during the month. What remains is the balance in the hands of the petty cashier.

slides.heading: Balancing the book and the reimbursement
bullets: Total the **Total** column and every analysis column; the heads must add up to the total.
Balance carried down = **imprest − total payments**.
Reimbursement = **total payments**, so balance plus reimbursement equals the imprest.

rows: Balance in hand at the start
Brought down from the last period

visual.alt: Table of the imprest of Tanjore Brass Emporium restored: balance in hand plus the reimbursement equals the imprest
visual.caption: Why the float comes back to the imprest

slides.narration: After the last voucher the book is totalled. The analysis columns must add up to the total payments. The balance carried down is the imprest less the payments. The head cashier reimburses exactly the payments. In our case rupees five hundred thirty five plus rupees one thousand four hundred sixty five equals rupees two thousand, the imprest. The cycle can start again.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a month with split vouchers
slides.body_md: **Bargarh Handloom House**, an imagined firm, has an imprest of ₹5,000 and ₹380 in hand on 1 February 2028. Voucher 15 is for printing ₹480 and postage ₹120. Prepare the book for the month.
bullets: Cash received ₹4,620; payments ₹4,085.
Balance carried down ₹915; reimbursement on 1 March ₹4,085.

rows: By Bus and auto fares of the salesman
By Repair of the weighing scale
By Printing of bill books and stamps
By Train fare to the exhibition
By Repair of the shop door lock

visual.alt: Analytical petty cash book of Bargarh Handloom House for February 2028 with an imprest of five thousand rupees: eight vouchers, one of them split over printing and postage, total payments of four thousand eighty five rupees and a balance of nine hundred fifteen rupees carried down
visual.caption: Bargarh Handloom House: imprest ₹5,000

slides.narration: The petty cashier has rupees three hundred eighty, and the head cashier gives rupees four thousand six hundred twenty to make the imprest of rupees five thousand. Eight vouchers are entered, and voucher fifteen is split between printing and postage. Payments total rupees four thousand eighty five. The balance carried down is rupees nine hundred fifteen, and the reimbursement is rupees four thousand eighty five.

slides.heading: Posting the petty cash book
bullets: Each **column total** is debited to its expense account.
The **reimbursement** is entered by the head cashier on the payment side of the cash book.
The debits and the credit are equal: the **total payments**.

rows: Reimbursement paid to the petty cashier

visual.alt: Posting of the petty cash book of Tanjore Brass Emporium: each expense account is debited with its column total and cash is credited with the reimbursement of one thousand four hundred sixty five rupees, so the debits and credits both come to one thousand four hundred sixty five rupees
visual.caption: Posting the column totals

slides.narration: At the end of the period each analysis column total is debited to its own expense account. The head cashier enters the reimbursement of rupees one thousand four hundred sixty five on the payment side of the cash book. The debits to the five expense accounts equal that single credit, so the double entry is complete without posting each voucher.

slides.heading: The purchases book: what goes in it
slides.body_md: The **purchases book** records only **credit purchases of goods** in which the firm deals. Cash purchases, assets and returns belong elsewhere.

rows: Goods bought on credit for resale
Machinery or furniture bought on credit

visual.alt: Table sorting four transactions: only credit purchases of goods for resale go to the purchases book; cash purchases go to the cash book, assets bought on credit go to the journal proper and returns go to the purchases return book

slides.narration: The purchases book records one thing only: goods bought on credit for resale. A cash purchase goes to the cash book. Machinery or furniture bought on credit is an asset and goes to the journal proper. Goods sent back to a supplier go to the purchases return book. The entry is made from the invoice received.

slides.heading: Format of the purchases book and trade discount
bullets: Columns: date, invoice number, name of supplier, **L.F.**, amount.
**Trade discount** is deducted from the list price on the invoice; only the **net amount** is entered.
No separate account is kept for trade discount.

visual.alt: Purchases book of Karaikudi Cycle Mart for March 2028: five credit purchases of one lakh fourteen thousand seven hundred rupees in all, each entered at the amount after trade discount
visual.caption: Simple purchases book

slides.narration: The purchases book has columns for the date, the invoice number, the name of the supplier, the ledger folio and the amount. The amount is the net figure. Trade discount is allowed on the invoice itself, so it never gets an account. Only the price after the discount is a transaction, and that is what the book shows.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: from invoices to the purchases book
slides.body_md: **Karaikudi Cycle Mart**, an imagined firm, received five invoices in March 2028. Find the net amount of each and total the book.
bullets: Trade discount on the list price of ₹1,27,500 is ₹12,800.
Net purchases of ₹1,14,700 are debited to Purchases A/c.

visual.alt: Working for the purchases book of Karaikudi Cycle Mart: list price, trade discount and net amount of each invoice, with a total list price of one lakh twenty seven thousand five hundred rupees, trade discount of twelve thousand eight hundred rupees and net purchases of one lakh fourteen thousand seven hundred rupees
visual.caption: Only the net column goes to the book

slides.narration: Work out each invoice first. Take the list price, deduct the trade discount, and what remains is the net amount. The invoices total rupees one lakh twenty seven thousand five hundred at list price. The discount is rupees twelve thousand eight hundred. The purchases book total is therefore rupees one lakh fourteen thousand seven hundred, the figure debited to Purchases.

slides.heading: Quick check: the net amount
slides.body_md: Deduct trade discount from the list price.
slides.narration: Find the discount as a percentage of the list price and take it away. The result is the amount that the purchases book shows.

slides.heading: The columnar purchases book
slides.body_md: A trader who buys several kinds of goods keeps a **column for each class** and a **total** column. Each invoice is split among the columns, so the month's purchases of each class are known at once.

visual.alt: First lines of a columnar purchases book of Haldia Fabric House, an imagined firm: date, invoice number, supplier, folio, a column each for cotton, silk and woollen goods and a total column
visual.caption: Format of the columnar purchases book (first lines only)

slides.narration: A trader who buys different kinds of goods can keep a column for each class, followed by a total column. Each invoice is split among the columns after trade discount. At the end of the month the column totals show purchases of each class, and they add up to the grand total, which gives a built in check.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a columnar purchases book
slides.body_md: **Haldia Fabric House**, an imagined firm, buys cotton, silk and woollen goods. Four invoices in April 2028 carry different trade discounts. Enter them with a column for each kind of goods.
bullets: Column totals: cotton ₹92,000, silk ₹58,000, woollen ₹78,500.
They add up to the total ₹2,28,500.

visual.alt: Columnar purchases book of Haldia Fabric House for April 2028: four invoices, with cotton ninety two thousand rupees, silk fifty eight thousand rupees and woollen goods seventy eight thousand five hundred rupees, a total of two lakh twenty eight thousand five hundred rupees
visual.caption: Columnar purchases book after trade discount

slides.narration: Each invoice is split into its three classes after the trade discount, and the invoice total is shown on the right. The cotton column totals rupees ninety two thousand, the silk column rupees fifty eight thousand and the woollen column rupees seventy eight thousand five hundred. Together they make rupees two lakh twenty eight thousand five hundred, which agrees with the total column.

slides.heading: The sales book and how it mirrors the purchases book
slides.body_md: The **sales book** is written from the **copy of the invoice** sent to the customer. It has the same layout, with the name of the customer, and is also kept in a columnar form.

rows: Copy of the invoice sent to the customer

visual.alt: Table comparing the purchases book and the sales book on what they record, source document, party column, posting of invoices and of the total, and trade discount

slides.narration: The sales book is the mirror image of the purchases book. It records credit sales of goods, written from the firm's own copy of the invoice. Cash sales go to the cash book, and the sale of an old asset goes to the journal proper. Trade discount is deducted in the same way, and a columnar form is possible for different classes of goods.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: a sales book
slides.body_md: **Shillong Hardware Works**, an imagined firm, made five credit sales in May 2028, each with its own trade discount. Prepare the sales book.
bullets: List price ₹1,23,500 less trade discount ₹10,500 gives net sales of ₹1,13,000.

visual.alt: Sales book of Shillong Hardware Works for May 2028: five credit sales to three customers, totalling one lakh thirteen thousand rupees after trade discount
visual.caption: Sales book of an imagined firm

slides.narration: The five invoices are entered at net amounts. At list price they come to rupees one lakh twenty three thousand five hundred, from which trade discount of rupees ten thousand five hundred is deducted. The sales book total is rupees one lakh thirteen thousand. This total will be credited to the Sales account, while each invoice is debited to the account of its customer.

slides.heading: Posting the day books to the ledger
bullets: Each **invoice** is posted to the **debit of the customer** with the folio **SB 1**, naming Sales A/c.
The **book total** ₹1,13,000 is posted once to the **credit of Sales A/c**.
In the purchases book everything is reversed: supplier credited, Purchases A/c debited.

visual.alt: Account of Jorhat Builders in the ledger of Shillong Hardware Works after the sales book is posted: the opening balance of fifteen thousand rupees and two invoices on the debit side, each with the folio SB 1
visual.caption: Posted, not yet balanced

slides.narration: Posting has two parts. Each invoice goes to the account of the customer, on the debit side, with the particulars To Sales and the folio of the sales book. At the month end the book total goes once to the credit of the Sales account. For the purchases book the sides are reversed: suppliers are credited and the Purchases account is debited.

slides.heading: Quick check: columns and totals
slides.body_md: What must the column totals add up to?
slides.narration: Think about how every invoice is shown twice in a columnar book, once in its goods column and once in the total column.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Fixed float; the amount spent is reimbursed; the float is restored
Total column and a column for each head; the column totals equal the total payments
Each head account debited with its column total; cash credited with the reimbursement
Credit transactions in goods only; trade discount deducted; net amount entered
A column for each class of goods; the column totals add up to the book total
Each invoice to the party account; the book total to Purchases A/c or Sales A/c

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: the imprest system, the analytical petty cash book, posting of petty cash, purchases and sales books, the columnar form and posting

slides.narration: To sum up. Under the imprest system the petty cashier holds a fixed sum, and the amount spent is reimbursed. The analytical book analyses payments by head, and the column totals are posted to the expense accounts. The purchases and sales books record credit transactions in goods only, at net amounts, and are posted by invoice and by total.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Write **receipts on the left**, with the opening balance and the cash received, and make both sides total the **imprest** or the same figure.
Check that the **analysis columns add up to the Total column** before balancing.
Enter **net amounts** in the purchases and sales books; show the list price and discount only in your working.
Leave out **cash transactions and assets**: say where they are recorded if the question asks.
slides.narration: In the examination, write the receipts on the left with the opening balance and the cash received. Check that the analysis columns add up to the total column before you balance. In the purchases and sales books enter only net amounts, and keep list prices for your working. Leave out cash transactions and assets, and say where they belong.

decks.title: Special Purpose Books — Part 2: Returns Books, Journal Proper and Posting
goals: State who issues a debit note and a credit note and when, and record returns in the purchases return book and the sales return book
Identify the entries recorded in the journal proper and pass opening, closing, rectifying, bad debt, drawings and credit-asset entries
Post the special books and the journal proper to the ledger and check that every account agrees with the book totals

slides.heading: Returns books, journal proper and posting
slides.body_md: Part 2: the **purchases return** and **sales return** books with **debit and credit notes**, the **journal proper**, and **posting** from the special books to the ledger.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: returns are recorded in the returns books from debit and credit notes, other entries go to the journal proper, and everything is posted to the ledger
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: Welcome to the second part. Goods are sometimes sent back, and the firm needs books and documents for that. Some transactions fit no special book at all, and those go to the journal proper. We close by posting everything to the ledger. All firms and figures here are imagined.

slides.heading: Debit note and credit note
slides.body_md: When goods are returned, a note tells the other party which of his accounts has changed.

rows: Goods are sent back to the supplier
Goods are taken back from the customer
His account is debited in the books of the buyer
His account is credited in the books of the seller
Purchases return book of the buyer
Sales return book of the seller

visual.alt: Table distinguishing a debit note from a credit note on who issues it, to whom, when, what it tells the receiver and the book in which it is recorded

slides.narration: A debit note is issued by the buyer to the supplier when goods are sent back. It tells the supplier that his account is debited in the buyer's books. A credit note is issued by the seller to the customer when goods are taken back, and it tells the customer that his account is credited. Each firm then records the return in its own book.

slides.heading: What a debit note contains
slides.body_md: The note names the **goods returned**, the **quantity and rate** and the **reason**. When goods bought at a trade discount are returned, the discount is allowed again, and the **net value** is the amount of the note.

rows: Karaikudi Cycle Mart (buyer), an imagined firm
Cycles, defective frames (as noted on the goods)

visual.alt: Specimen of a debit note issued by Karaikudi Cycle Mart to Vinayak Cycle Co. for goods returned with a list price of four thousand rupees, a trade discount of four hundred rupees and a debit note amount of three thousand six hundred rupees
visual.caption: What a debit note shows

slides.narration: A debit note gives its number and date, the name of the supplier, the goods returned with quantity, rate and reason, and the amount. If the goods were bought at a trade discount, the same discount is deducted again. Here the list price of rupees four thousand less rupees four hundred gives a note of rupees three thousand six hundred.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: the purchases return book
slides.body_md: **Karaikudi Cycle Mart**, an imagined firm, returned defective goods to two suppliers in March 2028, with a debit note each time. Enter the notes in the purchases return book.
bullets: Net value of the three notes: ₹8,450.
The total is posted to the **credit of Purchases Return A/c**; each note to the **debit of the supplier**.

visual.alt: Purchases return book of Karaikudi Cycle Mart for March 2028: three debit notes to two suppliers totalling eight thousand four hundred fifty rupees after trade discount
visual.caption: Purchases return book

slides.narration: The three debit notes are entered at net value, after the same trade discount that was allowed on the purchase. They total rupees eight thousand four hundred fifty. The suppliers are debited, because the firm owes them less. The total is credited once to the Purchases Return account at the month end.

slides.heading: Quick check: the returning document
slides.body_md: Who prepares the note when goods are sent back?
slides.narration: Think about who is returning the goods and which of his documents informs the supplier.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: the sales return book
slides.body_md: **Shillong Hardware Works**, an imagined firm, took back goods from two customers in May 2028 and issued a credit note each time. Prepare the sales return book.
bullets: Net value of the three credit notes: ₹8,100.
The total is posted to the **debit of Sales Return A/c**; each note to the **credit of the customer**.

visual.alt: Sales return book of Shillong Hardware Works for May 2028: three credit notes to two customers totalling eight thousand one hundred rupees after trade discount
visual.caption: Sales return book

slides.narration: The three credit notes are entered at net value. They total rupees eight thousand one hundred. Each customer's account is credited, because he now owes less. At the month end the total is debited once to the Sales Return account. Sales return is the opposite of sales, and purchases return is the opposite of purchases.

slides.heading: What returns do to a ledger account
bullets: A return **reduces** the balance of the party account.
A supplier's account is **debited** by a return; a customer's account is **credited**.
Each posting carries the folio of the return book, such as **PRB 1**.

visual.alt: Account of Vinayak Cycle Co. in the ledger of Karaikudi Cycle Mart: the opening balance and two purchases on the credit side, two returns on the debit side and a credit balance of eighty two thousand nine hundred fifty rupees carried down
visual.caption: Returns reduce what is owed to the supplier

slides.narration: Look at the account of a supplier. It opens with a credit balance, and credit purchases are added on the credit side. Each return is a debit and so reduces what is owed. After the two purchases and two returns the balance carried down is rupees eighty two thousand nine hundred fifty, a credit balance, still payable to the supplier.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: net purchases and net sales
slides.body_md: Returns are not a separate profit or loss; they **reduce** the purchases or sales of the period. The two day-book totals and the two returns totals give the net figures for the final accounts.

visual.alt: Net purchases of one lakh six thousand two hundred fifty rupees for Karaikudi Cycle Mart after deducting purchases returns, and net sales of one lakh four thousand nine hundred rupees for Shillong Hardware Works after deducting sales returns
visual.caption: Returns are deducted from the totals

slides.narration: For the cycle firm, purchases of rupees one lakh fourteen thousand seven hundred less returns of rupees eight thousand four hundred fifty leave net purchases of rupees one lakh six thousand two hundred fifty. For the hardware firm, sales of rupees one lakh thirteen thousand less returns of rupees eight thousand one hundred leave net sales of rupees one lakh four thousand nine hundred. These net figures go to the Trading Account later.

slides.heading: The journal proper
slides.body_md: The **journal proper** records every transaction for which **no special book exists**. It is a book of original entry like the others, with narration under each entry.

rows: Asset A/c Dr to the supplier
The buyer Dr to Asset A/c
Bad Debts A/c Dr to the debtor
Drawings A/c Dr to Purchases A/c
Goods lost by fire or theft
Loss A/c Dr to Purchases A/c
Passed once, at the start or end of the year
The corrected account is debited or credited

visual.alt: Table of transactions recorded in the journal proper with the entry for each: assets on credit, bad debts, goods withdrawn, goods lost, opening and closing entries and rectification

slides.narration: The journal proper takes what the other books leave out. A credit purchase or sale of an asset, a bad debt written off, goods taken by the proprietor, a loss of goods, the opening entry, the closing entries and rectifying entries all belong here. Each entry has a date, the debit and credit lines, and a narration.

slides.heading: Which book? Sorting a month of transactions
slides.body_md: Ask three questions: Is it **cash**? Is it a **credit purchase or sale of goods**? Is it a **return**? If none applies, use the **journal proper**.

rows: Bought goods on credit from Ravi Timbers, list price ₹60,000, trade discount 10%
Sold goods on credit to Meena Interiors, list price ₹40,000, trade discount 5%
Bought office computers on credit from Digital Mart for ₹45,000
Returned goods to Ravi Timbers, list price ₹5,000, trade discount 10%
Meena Interiors returned goods, list price ₹4,000, trade discount 5%
Proprietor took goods of ₹6,000 for his house
Wrote off ₹2,500 due from Deepak Fabricators as a bad debt
Sold goods on credit to Tarun Decor for ₹25,000, no trade discount
Sold old furniture on credit to Ravi Timbers for ₹8,000
Bought goods on credit from Ravi Timbers, list price ₹30,000, trade discount 10%

visual.alt: Transactions of Silchar Furnishings, an imagined firm, in January 2028, each with the book of first entry: credit purchases and sales, the two returns books, the cash book for cash transactions and the journal proper for the rest
visual.caption: Which book? A mixed month

slides.narration: To sort a transaction, ask three questions. Is cash involved? Then it is a matter for the cash book. Is it goods bought or sold on credit? Then use the purchases or sales book. Is it goods returned? Then use a returns book. If none of these fits, the transaction goes to the journal proper. The table shows a month sorted this way.

slides.heading: Quick check: which book?
slides.body_md: An asset is sold on credit.
slides.narration: Decide whether the thing sold is goods in which the firm deals, and whether any cash changes hands.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: assets on credit and a bad debt
slides.body_md: **Tezpur Paper Mart**, an imagined firm, buys machinery on credit, sells old furniture on credit at book value and writes off a debtor who is insolvent. Pass the journal proper entries.

rows: *(Being machinery bought on credit from Orient Engineers)*
*(Being old furniture sold on credit to Pradeep Stores at book value)*
*(Being the amount due from Mohan Sen written off as he is insolvent)*

visual.alt: Three journal proper entries of Tezpur Paper Mart, an imagined firm: machinery bought on credit, old furniture sold on credit at book value, and a debtor's balance written off as bad
visual.caption: Assets on credit and bad debts

slides.narration: Machinery bought on credit is debited to the machinery account and credited to the supplier. Furniture sold on credit at its book value debits the buyer and credits the furniture account. A bad debt debits the bad debts account, which is an expense, and credits the debtor, whose balance is removed. Each entry balances and carries its narration.

slides.heading: Goods withdrawn, lost or given away
bullets: Goods taken by the proprietor: **Drawings A/c Dr**.
Goods destroyed by fire: **Loss by Fire A/c Dr**.
Free samples: **Advertisement A/c Dr**.
In every case **Purchases A/c is credited** at cost.

rows: *(Being goods taken by the proprietor for personal use)*
*(Being goods destroyed by fire, no insurance claim)*
*(Being goods given away as free samples)*

visual.alt: Three journal proper entries of Tezpur Paper Mart: goods taken by the proprietor debited to Drawings, goods destroyed by fire debited to Loss by Fire and goods given as free samples debited to Advertisement, each credited to Purchases
visual.caption: Goods leave the stock without a sale

slides.narration: Sometimes goods leave the stock without a sale. If the proprietor takes them, debit drawings. If fire destroys them, debit the loss. If they are given as free samples, debit advertisement. In every case credit purchases at cost, because the goods are no longer available for sale. Nothing is entered in the sales book, since no sale has taken place.

slides.heading: The opening entry
slides.body_md: When new books begin, an **opening entry** debits every asset and credits every liability. **Capital** is the balancing figure: assets less liabilities.

rows: *(Being the assets, liabilities and capital of the firm brought into the new books)*

visual.alt: Opening entry of Tezpur Paper Mart dated 1 April 2028: assets debited, the creditor and the loan credited, and capital of two lakh sixty five thousand rupees as the balancing figure
visual.caption: Capital is the balancing figure

slides.narration: At the start of new books, an opening entry brings in the old balances. Every asset is debited. The creditor and the loan are credited. The difference is the capital of the proprietor. Here the assets are rupees three lakh seventy five thousand and the liabilities rupees one lakh ten thousand, so capital is rupees two lakh sixty five thousand.

sections.heading: 1. Special purpose books
sections.body_md:
A trader who recorded every transaction in a single journal would repeat the same entries again and again. Transactions of one kind are therefore grouped in a **special purpose (subsidiary) book**, which is totalled periodically so that only the totals need be posted.

- **Petty cash book:** small cash payments.
- **Purchases book** and **sales book:** credit purchases and credit sales of goods.
- **Purchases return book** and **sales return book:** goods sent back to suppliers and taken back from customers.
- **Journal proper:** every transaction for which no special book exists.

The cash book is the subject of Chapter 5. Transactions involving GST are not examined in Class XI Accounts.

sections.heading: 2. Petty cash and the imprest system
sections.body_md:
**Petty cash** pays for small items such as postage, fares, stationery and refreshments. The **petty cashier** keeps it and writes the **petty cash book**; the **head cashier** supplies the cash.

Under the **imprest system**:

1. The head cashier gives the petty cashier a **fixed sum, the imprest**, at the start of the period.
2. The petty cashier pays against **vouchers** and records each.
3. At the end of the period the book is totalled and balanced.
4. The head cashier **reimburses exactly the amount spent**, so the petty cashier again holds the imprest.

The control is simple: the imprest is the limit, and each reimbursement is backed by vouchers.

sections.heading: 3. The analytical petty cash book: format, balancing and posting
sections.body_md:
**Format.** The left side is the **receipts** column (balance in hand and cash received). To the right are date, particulars, **voucher number**, a **Total** column of payments and an **analysis column** for each head, such as postage, stationery, conveyance, refreshments and sundries.

Each payment is written in the Total column and again in its head; a voucher of two heads is split. **Balancing:** total the Total column and every analysis column (the heads must add up to the total payments); write the balance carried down on the payment side so both sides equal the imprest; bring it down below with the reimbursement.

**Posting:** debit each expense account with its column total; credit Cash with the reimbursement. Debits and credit are equal.

sections.heading: 4. Purchases book and sales book: simple and columnar
sections.body_md:
The **purchases book** records **credit purchases of goods** only, from the invoice received; the **sales book** records **credit sales of goods** only, from the copy of the invoice sent. Cash transactions go to the cash book; assets bought or sold on credit go to the journal proper; returns go to the returns books.

**Trade discount** is deducted from the list price on the invoice, so only the **net amount** is entered: net = list price − trade discount. It is not entered in any account. **Cash discount** depends on prompt payment and is recorded in the cash book, not here.

**Columnar form:** a column for each class of goods and a total column; the column totals must add up to the book total, and each can be posted to its own goods account (for example Cotton Purchases A/c).

sections.heading: 5. Returns books, debit notes and credit notes
sections.body_md:
When the **buyer** returns goods he sends the supplier a **debit note**; the supplier's account is debited in the buyer's books. When the **seller** takes goods back he sends the customer a **credit note**; the customer's account is credited in the seller's books.

- **Purchases return book** (buyer): entered from debit notes at net value; **total credited to Purchases Return A/c**, each note debited to the supplier.
- **Sales return book** (seller): entered from credit notes at net value; **total debited to Sales Return A/c**, each note credited to the customer.

Goods returned for an immediate cash refund are cash transactions.

sections.heading: 6. The journal proper
sections.body_md:
The journal proper records transactions that no special book can take. The common entries are:

- **Credit purchase of an asset:** Asset A/c Dr to the supplier.
- **Credit sale of an asset:** the buyer Dr to the Asset A/c.
- **Bad debts:** Bad Debts A/c Dr to the debtor.
- **Goods withdrawn by the proprietor:** Drawings A/c Dr to Purchases A/c (at cost).
- **Goods lost by fire or theft, or given as free samples:** Loss (or Advertisement) A/c Dr to Purchases A/c; an insurance claim admitted is debited separately.
- **Opening entry:** assets Dr, liabilities and capital Cr; capital = assets − liabilities.
- **Closing (transfer) entries:** for example Trading A/c Dr to Purchases A/c.
- **Rectifying entries:** the wrong account is credited and the right one debited.

Every entry carries a narration.

sections.heading: 7. Posting from the special books to the ledger
sections.body_md:
Posting follows one pattern:

- The **personal account** gets **each** invoice or note (the debit or credit of the party).
- The **goods account** gets the **book total** (or each column total) once, with the particulars "Sundries as per the book".
- The **journal proper** has no total: each entry is posted to every account it names.

The folio in the ledger names the source and page: **PB** purchases book, **SB** sales book, **PRB** purchases return book, **SRB** sales return book, **J** journal proper. A check at the end: the total posted to the personal accounts equals the total posted to the goods accounts equals the book total.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are usually split (ISC Accounts, Section A)**
- 1 mark: one correct option, the issuer of a debit or credit note, or the book of first entry.
- 2 marks: the meaning of the imprest system, a distinction between a debit and a credit note, or two journal proper entries with narration.
- 3 marks: a purchases, sales or returns book from invoices, a supplier's or customer's account posted and balanced, or three journal proper entries.
- 5 marks: an analytical petty cash book with the reimbursement, a columnar day book with its posting, or a mixed list of transactions sorted into books with the journal proper entries.

**Step marks** usually go for each correct net amount, each column or book total, each account posted on its correct side, the balance carried down, and the narration.

**Common mistakes**
- Entering list price instead of the net amount after trade discount.
- Putting a cash purchase, or the credit purchase of furniture, in the purchases book.
- Letting the analysis columns of the petty cash book disagree with the Total column.
- Reimbursing the imprest instead of the amount spent.
- Mixing up the debit note (buyer) and the credit note (seller), or posting the returns to the wrong side.
- Forgetting to credit Purchases when goods are withdrawn by the proprietor or lost.

questions.stem_md: Sundar Rice Mills, an imagined firm, gives its petty cashier the same fixed sum at the start of every week and, at the week end, pays him exactly the amount he has spent. This method of keeping petty cash is called the

options.text_md: cash discount system
imprest system
columnar cash system
contra system

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** imprest system. A fixed float that is topped up by the amount spent is the imprest system. A cash discount is an allowance for early payment, a contra entry moves funds between cash and bank, and no system named columnar cash exists.

questions.stem_md: What does an analytical petty cash book kept by Palani Dairy Products, an imagined firm, show that a petty cash book with a single amount column does not?

options.text_md: The payments sorted by customer and by supplier
The balance of the bank account after each payment
The profit made on each voucher
The payments sorted into columns by the head of expense, with a total for each head

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The payments sorted into columns by the head of expense, with a total for each head. The analysis columns collect like expenses together, so that a column total can be posted to its expense account. Customers, the bank balance and profit are outside a petty cash book.

questions.stem_md: The imprest of Sundar Rice Mills is ₹3,000. In a week its petty cashier paid ₹380 on postage, ₹745 on stationery, ₹615 on conveyance and ₹500 on sundries. At the week end the head cashier must reimburse
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** ₹2,240. Payments = 380 + 745 + 615 + 500 = 2,240, and the reimbursement equals the payments. ₹760 is only the balance still in the petty cashier's hands, ₹3,000 is the imprest itself, and ₹5,240 wrongly adds the imprest to the payments.

questions.stem_md: At the end of the month, the Stationery column total of the analytical petty cash book of Warangal Cold Stores, an imagined firm, is posted to the ledger by

options.text_md: crediting Stationery A/c
debiting Petty Cash A/c with the same amount
debiting Stationery A/c
crediting Purchases A/c

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** debiting Stationery A/c. Stationery is an expense, so its column total is posted to the debit of the Stationery account. Crediting it would reduce the expense, the cash credit is made once for the whole reimbursement, and Purchases has no part in a petty expense.

questions.stem_md: The petty cashier of Vidisha Plywood, an imagined firm, starts a month with ₹5,000, which is the imprest. After spending ₹3,640 during the month, the amount left with him is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** ₹1,360. Balance in hand = 5,000 − 3,640 = ₹1,360. The ₹3,640 is the amount spent and to be reimbursed, ₹5,000 is the imprest before any spending, and the sum ₹8,640 cannot be in hand.

questions.stem_md: A petty voucher of Dhenkanal Papers, an imagined firm, is for ₹180: a courier charge of ₹60 and ₹120 for the packing tape. How should it be entered in the analytical petty cash book that has Postage, Stationery and Sundries columns?

₹180 in the Total column and ₹180 under Sundries only
₹60 in the Total column and ₹120 under Sundries
₹180 in the Total column and nothing in any analysis column

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** ₹180 in the Total column, ₹60 under Postage and ₹120 under Sundries. The total column carries the whole voucher and the analysis columns split it by head, so the column totals later equal the total of the payments. Putting all of it under Sundries misstates the postage, entering only ₹60 loses part of the payment, and leaving the analysis blank means no expense account is debited.
